messages.subject: Pairwise Amova
parts:
Hello again, 
I am working with 3 populations and, to explore the genetic structure among and between populations, I performed an AMOVA using poppr.amova, which also provide a PhI-stat.  

Now, I was wondering how can I do this pairwise, to determine which pair of populations pair is the most differentiated and obtain a pairwise index of population differentiation PHI-pt. 

I guess, I can subset my dataset and perform the AMOVA by pair, but I'm not sure this is the most appropriate way to do this.  

Again, many thanks 

RV

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Pairwise Amova
parts:
At the moment, there is no feature to do this automatically in part because it gets complex when you introduce hierarchy into the mix.

There are alternatives that you might try that would give you the same kind of information you are looking for:

1. Create a bootstrapped tree from distances between populations using aboot(data, ~pop) (https://grunwaldlab.github.io/poppr/reference/aboot.html)

2. Use DAPC to create a visualization showing how the populations relate to each other in 2-D space (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/thibautjombart/adegenet/master/tutorials/tutorial-dapc.pdf)

3. If you have diploid data, you can also calculate pairwise Fst via the {hierfstat} package https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/hierfstat/versions/0.5-7/topics/pairwise.neifst https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/hierfstat/versions/0.5-7/topics/pairwise.WCfst

Hope that helps.

Best,
Zhian

messages.author: d192ec4b1d416345
messages.subject: Re: [poppr] Pairwise Amova
parts:
I don't think it's terribly necessary. The DAPC shows visually what the AMOVA is doing (albiet, using a slightly different method of input data). Doing a pairwise AMOVA would only reduce your degrees of freedom and won't really tell you anything new.

We used DAPC to bolster the AMOVA results for our analyses back in 2017: "When we analyze the AMOVA results in light of the DAPC results (Fig. 5), it becomes clear that the regional patterns of differentiation are largely driven by isolates from Mexico and CA." (https://peerj.com/articles/4152/).

Best,
Zhian
